For each new or updated article, emit a block:

===ARTICLE concepts/<slug>.md===
<full markdown: complete YAML frontmatter + body, per the AGENTS.md schema>
===END ARTICLE===

Use `connections/<slug>.md` for connection articles and `qa/<slug>.md` for Q&A.
Slugs are lowercase and hyphenated. To UPDATE an existing article, emit it with
its existing path and the full revised content (it overwrites).

After the article blocks, emit exactly one index block and one log block:

===INDEX===
| [[concepts/<slug>]] | one-line summary | 2026-10-22.md | 2026-10-22 |
===END INDEX===

===LOG===
## [2026-10-22T23:02:29-05:00] compile | 2026-10-22.md
- Source: daily/2026-10-22.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/<slug>]]
- Articles updated: (none)
===END LOG===

### Rules
1. Identify 3-7 distinct concepts worth their own article.
2. Emit ===NOTHING=== ONLY when the log itself contains no durable knowledge
   (e.g. "FLUSH_OK", or purely transient chatter). "An article already covers
   this topic" is NOT a reason to emit ===NOTHING=== - it is a reason to UPDATE
   that article with whatever this log adds.
3. Every article: complete YAML frontmatter (title, sources, created, updated)
   with `sources` citing 2026-10-22.md; at least 2 [[wikilinks]]; Key Points
   3-5 bullets; Details 2+ paragraphs; Related Concepts 2+ entries; encyclopedia
   style — neutral and comprehensive. Follow the AGENTS.md article format exactly.
4. Create a connection article when the log reveals a non-obvious relationship
   between 2+ concepts.
4b. Do NOT re-emit an article whose only change would be the `updated:` date or
   a restatement of what it already says. Measured on a real run, 4 of 5
   "updates" changed nothing but the timestamp - that is churn: it rewrites
   files, dirties backups, and invalidates caches while adding no knowledge.
   Re-emit an article only when you are adding substantive content.
5. Add one ===INDEX=== table row per article (new or updated).

Emit ONLY the delimiter blocks — no preamble, no commentary.

message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.


## Current Wiki Index

# Knowledge Base Index

# Google Drive Dedupe by API Content Hash (drive_index.py and the Flint Checksum Move)

On 2026-10-22 several sessions worked on cleaning up Eric's Google Drive. The Drive is 5 TB with 1.0 TB used, so space was not the issue. All of them matched duplicates by the Drive API's `md5Checksum` and not by filename. Every earlier check had matched by name only, because reading through the Mac's Drive mount hangs. One session built a read-only index and search tool, `~/DEV/_INBOX/tools/drive_index.py`. Another moved 3,699 confirmed duplicates (about 50 GB) into `_TO_REVIEW` and deleted nothing. The evening closeout added a `_TO_REVIEW` zone to the index and a new `tools/trash_review.py`, and logged a first trash wave in `trash_log_2026-10-22.csv`.

## Key Points

- **Duplicates are matched by content fingerprint, not by name.** The API's md5 check avoids the FUSE mount hang and finds real twins even when their names differ. Before any bulk move, two sample pairs were downloaded and hashed locally, and one test move was run.
- **The first index scanned 614,290 items.** It found 106,560 old copies (172 GB) whose exact twin sits in a folder Eric keeps. Some folders were 95–100% twins, such as `99_UNSORTED/From_REMOTE_DESK` at 54 GB. Others, like `From_Desktop` and `From_DropBox`, were mostly unique files and must not be trashed as a whole. `99_UNSORTED` turned out to be 76 GB, not the 23.8 GB recorded earlier.
- **The move happened and nothing was deleted.** 3,699 files moved, and each one's keep copy stayed in a top-priority Flint folder. Three groups were left where they were: 4,889 "tie" copies (both copies in a top-priority folder), 142,537 copies with no priority keep copy, and copies outside the move's scope. The move skipped Zotero copies, 1,049 native Google Docs (they have no checksum), and files that sit in two folders at once.
- **About 214k items had no My Drive path.** Most are old laptop backups in Drive's "Computers" section. Safety rule: before trashing one, confirm that neither the Mac nor the Windows laptop still syncs that folder through Drive for desktop. If one does, trashing the Drive copy could delete files on that laptop. The closeout added a concrete step: turn off the Windows laptop's Drive for desktop backup of `DEV` and check that the Mac's "My Mac" list is empty.
- **Trash happens in small reviewed waves.** Nothing goes to trash without Eric's OK. The next wave is one `_PARKED_COPIES` folder that is about 100% duplicates.

## Details

`drive_index.py` only reads. It stores a local index of every item in `_INBOX/drive-index/` (`drive.sqlite`, the report CSVs, and `trash_log_2026-10-22.csv`). That folder is kept out of git and stays on the Mac. `python3 -I tools/drive_index.py find <terms>` shows the best copy first, then a link and a copy count, and `--all` also lists backup copies. Search covers names only, not file contents. Two design choices matter. First, the index adds a `parent` folder-ID column, so a path that will not resolve can still be traced. The read queries name their columns, so adding a column did not break them. Second, a new index replaces the old one only after a full build finishes, so an interrupted rebuild leaves the previous index intact. That mattered the same day: Claude Code killed the background rebuild under memory pressure, and the rebuild (about 15 minutes) waits for free memory and for Eric to say "rebuild." The closeout commits were `f0b1268` in the thin `~/DEV` repo (plan Task 8, STATUS, and the handoff `docs/handoffs/2026-10-22-drive-index-and-first-trash-wave.md`) and `eb8bae6` in `~/DEV/_INBOX` (the index's `_TO_REVIEW` zone, `trash_review.py`, and STATUS).

The Flint session shows what this costs at full scale. Walking about 450K items took hours, mostly in `10_ARCHIVE` (176,337 items) and `OneDrive-Import` (137,521). Monitors repeatedly gave up after 30 minutes with no events. Each time, the agent checked progress again and did not start any moves. The logs (`move_log.csv`, `dup_plan.csv`) are in `~/DEV/Flint/data/drive_dedupe_2026-10-22/`. The checksum method has a hard limit: native Google Docs have no md5, so deduping them would need a different method. The tie copies show a second limit. When two identical copies both sit in top-priority folders, the hash cannot say which one to keep, so a person has to choose the keep folder. The recommended option is to leave ties and unmatched copies alone. The work is recorded as Task 8 in `~/DEV/docs/FILE-ORGANIZATION-PLAN.md`. The plan's earlier choice to leave `99_UNSORTED` untouched until 2027 was based on a wrong size and needs revisiting. Naming rules already exist in the Primary ladder `README.md`, and 549 names in the keep folders break them. Whether to rename those now or keep a "new files only" rule is an open decision.

# PFF Baylor 2026 QB Proof-of-Concept Report and Docs-to-Drive Copy

On 2026-10-22 two PFF_Data_Project sessions on the Mac did three things. They copied the project's 19 docs to `My Drive/PFF_endpoint/docs/`. They searched for a `pff_advanced_metrics` folder that did not exist. And they produced a Baylor 2026 quarterback report modeled on the existing O-line method. The report (`qb_poc_report.md`, plus `qb_player_game.csv` containing only aggregates) was written to `My Drive/PFF_endpoint/pff_advanced_metrics/`.

## Key Points

- **Scope: six graded Baylor games** (weeks 1–5 and 7), 8 QB player-game rows across 3 QBs, and 297 charted dropbacks. Week 13 returned no rows because it had not been graded yet.
- **Filter grade feeds by Baylor franchise `118` before counting.** The QB rows include opposing quarterbacks. The first milestone reported 16 rows, and it was corrected to 8 in the thread.
- **The modeling steps were skipped on purpose.** Elastic net, PLS, and a time-based split were not run, because with 8 graded rows the coefficients would mean nothing. The report says so. What it delivers instead is descriptive: per-dropback rates for each QB with bootstrap intervals, using the PFF offense grade as the outcome and pass grade as a check.
- **A token-like string is tracked on GitHub.** `docs/swagger/bearer-auth.yaml` contains an 854-character string in `erash11/PFF_Data_Project`. It was left out of the Drive copy, and its value was never printed. Eric needs to check whether it is live, rotate it if so, and scrub it from git history.
- **Option B (fit across all FBS QBs, then place Baylor's QBs in that model) needs Eric's OK**, because it goes beyond Baylor-only scope.

## Details

Several data facts came out of building the report. The local PFF database is DuckDB, not SQLite, and it holds Baylor grades only through week 3, so later weeks have to come from the API. `qb_charting` rows are nested under a `qb_charting` key, which held 565 rows covering both teams. The `all_routes` endpoint returns 404. The data owner has asked that datasets not be joined directly. The repo's existing API client, which handles the login token, was used read-only. The venv was placed in a scratch directory outside the repo because DuckDB was not installed and the system Python is PEP 668-managed. When an old DuckDB call failed, the schema file was read instead. When a `sed` edit failed, the script was rewritten with a heredoc. Before posting, the report's counts were checked against the CSV, which caught two wrong per-player game counts (184426 has 4 games and 184815 has 3). Accuracy is labeled with the FRA code rather than the word "accurate."

The secret check followed a specific method. The agent searched for matches but printed only their lengths, then located the file by those lengths, and never printed a value. Docs that describe bearer auth produce many harmless matches, so an unusually long string is the real signal. Both output files were scanned for tokens and keys before publishing, and the scan found nothing. Eric asked whether moving the docs to Drive would fix things. Drive helped only with the missing folder, since the Mac can see Drive. The report itself was blocked on a spec, and that was settled when Eric approved one in the thread.

# Kenny Boyd Status Loop: Teams-Hosted ITS Tracker and Wednesday Prep

On 2026-10-22 Eric set up a recurring status loop with Kenny Boyd for the SoftwareTech_Review project, built around the weekly Thursday 2:30 PM CT check-in. The biggest gap in the one-page plan was that Kenny could not open Eric's personal Google Drive. To fix that, the live ITS project tracker moved into the Files area of a private Microsoft Teams team, which required one approved exception to a standing rule. The same session finished a task-vs-goal audit and added five decision rules to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

## Key Points

- **There is one approved exception to "never Baylor OneDrive/SharePoint."** It covers the Files of the private team "Athletics Software & Technology Review," which holds the ITS tracker and, per TEAMS_PLAN.md, the costs workbook. Any other Baylor destination still needs Eric's OK. The exception is recorded in Tier A `feedback_no-baylor-onedrive.md`.
- **The Teams copy is now the live tracker.** The Drive copy `01_Working/ITS_Project_Tracker_ER_2026-10-01.xlsx` is retired and should not be edited. It is due to be renamed with a `_RETIRED_2026-10-22` suffix once Eric says "rename it."

- **Audit-derived rule:** when Eric proposes a solution, Claude restates the goal behind it, keeps his idea on the table, and names a better fit if one exists (commit `37faed4`).

Two live trackers would drift apart, so the old one gets a dated retired name rather than being left in place to confuse later sessions. The tracker's columns were left as they were. Its 14-day red flag depends on last-contact dates that have not been entered yet.

The task-vs-goal audit found that Jev can sort prompts but cannot rewrite them. Because the 1,071-prompt Jev run was blocked, the sort was done on the Mac. The resulting CLAUDE.md rule records a habit from the audit: treat a handed-over solution as evidence of the goal behind it, not as the goal itself. The SoftwareTech_Review repo has its own rules: no em dashes, and keep the "where everything lives" table up to date whenever a file moves. STATUS was updated in commits `107e2d9` and `f6e801b`. The plan page is published as a claude.ai artifact and was not tested in a browser preview. Whether to share it with Kenny is still open.

# Launchd cloud-push Fails With Operation Not Permitted While Manual Runs Work

The scheduled cloud copy `~/.claude/scripts/cloud-push.py` has failed under launchd since 2026-10-12 18:19, each time with "Operation not permitted". The same script works when run by hand from a terminal. The code is not at fault. The launchd job runs with different permissions from the interactive shell. A 2026-10-21 investigation found that the job uses a different Python from the shell, and that macOS's privacy layer (TCC) lets that Python read the Google Drive CloudStorage folder but not write to it. The fix is to give Full Disk Access to the exact binary the job runs, `/usr/bin/python3`. Eric has to do that by hand in System Settings. On 2026-10-22 it still had not been done, and a `kickstart` test failed the same way again.

## Key Points

- **If a job works by hand but fails on schedule, check the execution context before the code.** An interactive terminal holds TCC grants that a launchd job does not inherit.
- **A job can read a folder and still be unable to write to it.** On 2026-10-21, `ls` on the Drive folder worked while writes to `My Drive/_MACHINE/Cloud_Copy/DEV/` failed. On 2026-10-22 the 09:27 log entry showed `rsync exit 1` with `Operation not permitted` on that same folder.
- **The job and the shell use different interpreters.** `com.keystone.clouddrivepush` runs `/usr/bin/caffeinate -i /usr/bin/python3 .../cloud-push.py`, while the shell's `python3` is Homebrew 3.14. Full Disk Access has to be granted to `/usr/bin/python3`.
- **A wrapper's exit code is not the push result.** On 2026-10-22 a background wrapper exited 0 even though the push it started (06:42) had not finished. The wrapper only launched the push and tailed the log, so the push log is the only valid evidence of success.
- **When `launchctl bootstrap` fails with an I/O error, run `bootout` and then bootstrap again.** This error usually means a job with the same label is already loaded or stale.

## Details

This failure belongs to the same class as Windows Task Scheduler's minimal PATH and hook environments that differ from the interactive shell: the process environment is fixed at launch. On macOS that environment includes permissions as well as variables. A terminal with Full Disk Access passes the grant down to scripts it starts. A launchd agent is a separate responsible process and starts without any of those grants. A manual success therefore only shows that the code is correct.

The 2026-10-21 session found three things. First, `launchctl kickstart` reproduces the failure inside launchd's context, which a terminal run cannot do, so kickstart is the right test once the fix is in place. Second, writes failed while reads succeeded, so the denial depends on the operation and a read-only check can wrongly report that everything is fine. Third, the job's interpreter is not the shell's, which explains why earlier Full Disk Access attempts seemed to have no effect: granting access to Homebrew Python or to the terminal does not cover `/usr/bin/python3`. The handoff procedure has three steps. Add `/usr/bin/python3` under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access. Run `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.keystone.clouddrivepush`. Then check `tail -5 ~/.claude/scripts/logs/cloud-push.log`.

On 2026-10-22, two sessions picked the job up again. In the morning the status check found the last failed run at 10-21 17:30 and an overnight backup with 5 errors: global-memory had diverged, and 4 snapshot uploads had failed. After Eric said "go", one push was started. It ran past two minutes and was moved to the background, and its wrapper exited 0. The result was still unknown because the push itself had not finished. A later session, carrying Eric's own confirmation in the project thread at 14:26Z, restored the login catch-up job by copying `com.keystone.dailybackup-login.plist` into `~/Library/LaunchAgents/`. The first `bootstrap` returned an I/O error, and `bootout` followed by a second `bootstrap` loaded it. That session then ran a kickstart of the cloud push, which failed again. This confirms the permission grant had still not been made. One concern remains open: right after bootstrap, `launchctl print` showed the login job with `state = running`. If the plist sets `RunAtLoad`, loading it may have started a backup, which conflicts with the instruction not to run the backup. The plist needs to be checked. No permissions were changed by the agent in either session.

# Relayed Instructions and Blanket Grants Are Not User Consent

During the 2026-10-21 KeystoneOS repair session the agent applied a consent rule: a note relayed from a coordinator session does not count as approval for a specific consequential action, and neither does a broad grant like "you have full system access." Restoring a launchd plist Eric had deleted and writing to Google Drive both waited until Eric himself gave an unambiguous "yes." Permission changes such as Full Disk Access were left to Eric to make by hand. The next day the rule held in three more sessions, including one where the relay explicitly said "Eric approved these steps," and one where Eric's own message was itself ambiguous.

## Key Points

- **A relay note reports intent, so it is not consent.** On 2026-10-22 a relay saying "Eric approved these steps" was not acted on. The agent posted a question to the project thread, and the work went ahead only after Eric replied there himself at 14:26Z: "Yes, restore the login, catch up, and run one cloud push."
- **A blanket grant answers whether the agent can act. It does not answer whether it should.** "Full system access" does not name an action, so the agent asks which action the user means.
- **An ambiguous approval from the user still needs clarifying.** Eric's "your preapproved." during the PFF session could have covered a Drive copy or a QB report run. The agent asked "A or B?" and did not pick one.
- **Undoing something the user deliberately did needs fresh approval.** The deleted `dailybackup-login.plist` was restored only after Eric's explicit yes.
- **Privacy-permission changes stay manual.** The agent gives the exact binary path and the commands to verify. The human makes the TCC grant.

## Details

The rule matters more as work is split across coordinator and worker sessions. A relayed message loses who said it and exactly what they agreed to. "Eric approved these steps" could be a paraphrase, an inference, or a stale approval that came before a later decision. The 2026-10-22 morning session showed the standard working as intended: the agent did not re-run the cloud push off the automated relay, and waited for Eric's own "go." The 10:38 session took it one step further and sent the confirmation request to a channel Eric reads, so his answer is on record next to the work it authorized.

The PFF session showed a second failure mode. The words came from the user, but they did not say which action they covered. "your preapproved." could have authorized either of two different actions. Treating a real but ambiguous message as approval for the riskier reading would be the same mistake as trusting a relay. In practice, consent has to come from the user and also name the action it covers. When it does not, the agent asks a clarifying question and the action waits, which happened here because Eric did not answer. This builds on existing practice: pushes are scoped per repo, destructive git operations need authorization, and authorization is requested again when the diagnosis changes. The new part is a list of inputs that look like approval but are not: relay notes, capability statements, and approvals that do not say what they cover.

# Cloudroom Local vs Cloud Desks and the Mac-Only Stack After Windows Retirement

On 2026-10-14 Eric confirmed that Cloudroom, a tool for running agent threads on "desks," fits his routine. He had already started 42 threads by hand. In the same session he said the Windows laptop is retired and Docker is removed, so the Mac plus Google Drive is now the only working environment. That changed three earlier answers: whether to keep memsearch, when Cloudroom is used, and whether a VPS is allowed.

## Key Points

- **Data boundary:** Local desks are for work that should keep running on the Mac. Cloud desks are only for GitHub repos with no athlete data, such as PlayCalls_SuccessRate_EPA, the personal site and Signal Plays. DexaProject, GPS, VALD, force-plate work and anything on the Drive mount are never sent to Cloud.
- **Keep memsearch and Milvus Lite.** The two main problems behind a possible SQLite switch were Docker on Windows and Windows timeouts, and both are gone. The one remaining Mac lock issue is already handled by a wrapper.
- **Cloudroom is now an all-day tool.** A Cloud thread keeps running when the Mac is closed and a Local thread pauses, so Cloud desks matter more on a single laptop.
- **Staged adoption:** use Local desks only for two weeks and do lesson 1. After that, try one Cloud thread. The VPS decision comes last. Cloud servers and schedulers were approved on 2026-10-14, so self-hosting `cloudroom-core` is allowed but deferred.
- **Retirement has to reach the docs.** Memory was updated (Tier A note, its index line, two Tier B lines; PASS). `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, `machine.md` and the memory-write skill still describe two machines, and `Cloudroom_Learning/MISSION.md` still lists "Windows hands-off" and "needs Baylor IT approval."

## Details

The Cloud-desk rule applies the existing destination-split policy to a new kind of execution surface. Athlete-identifiable data already lives only on Drive and never on GitHub. A Cloud desk runs code on someone else's infrastructure, so it sits with GitHub, not with the local machine. The test is simple and checkable: a repo is eligible for Cloud only if it is on GitHub and has no athlete data. Anything that reads the Drive mount fails the test automatically.

Retiring Windows removed the constraint that shaped many past decisions, which is why answers given earlier had to be checked again. The memsearch decision turned around for this reason: the case for moving to SQLite rested on Windows-only failures, and with those gone, switching would be work with no current benefit. The other effect is documentation debt. Each file that still says "both machines are active" will steer later sessions toward cross-machine handling that no longer applies. Two edit attempts on `MISSION.md`, one through a Python heredoc and one through the Edit tool, were both blocked by the permission classifier. The next attempt is to be a plain command, and only after Eric says "edit the mission." The handoff for this session was written to a macOS temp folder, which repeats a known placement mistake.

# One Network Drop, Two Failures: Autopush Signal 9 and Dead Memory Flushes

On 2026-10-20 a session-start hook reported that `session-autopush` had failed 3 times at 05:06 UTC with "git-remote-https died of signal 9" while pushing DEV. A stack-doctor check found a second problem: 3 memory flushes had stopped and left their context files in `scripts/`. Both came from one short network drop at about 00:06 local time. Separately, `daily-backup` had failed 3 times between 10-15 and 10-19, and its 10-17 log said "Could not resolve host", so the Mac was offline then too.

## Key Points

- **Look for one host cause when failures arrive together.** An autopush failure and dead flushes at nearly the same time pointed to the network, not to two bugs.
- **"Signal 9" names the process that was killed, not why.** The push did not fail because of the repo; the transport stopped.
- **Repair was re-running, not rewriting.** A DEV fetch test passed, DEV was pulled (1 commit behind), and the 3 leftover flush context files were run by hand. All 3 saved to that day's daily log.
- **The error log was archived first, then cleared** to `.errors.log.archived-2026-10-20`, using `cp /dev/null` for truncation. A second check was clean.
- **One isolated old `flush-error` was left alone.** The 2026-10-18 "Control request timeout" did not repeat and only the compiler writes daily logs, so the file was not edited. A clean check exit is still not proof for every layer, so the entries were read.

## Details

The flush pipeline writes a context file before calling the model, so a network failure leaves a recoverable artifact on disk instead of a lost session. That is why recovery cost only three manual runs. The same principle shows up in other parts of the stack: write the expensive stage to disk before the fragile one.

The day had two conflicting positions on the error log. An earlier closeout said not to clear `.errors.log` until the failures were fixed. It listed 12 lines: 3 failed backups, compiler flush timeouts with a stale lock and backlog, a missing 10-17 GPS coach report PDF, and a failed claude-files digest email. Stack doctor later archived and cleared the log after confirming the network cause and re-running the flushes. The archive keeps the record, but the backup failures were only confirmed fixed if the next scheduled run succeeds. The 17:03 closeout set that test: after the 9 PM backup, `launchctl list | grep dailybackup` should show 0. The GPS coach report was retired the same day (23 files moved to `DataBase_GPS_Reporting/archive/coach_report/`, commit `4011885`), which settles the missing-PDF item.

# DEV Sync 2026-10-20: A Cloud-Created Repo, the _DRIVE Walk Hang, and Leftover Conflict Files

The Mac start-of-day `/dev-sync` on 2026-10-20 checked 145 repos. Six were pulled (PP_Recruiting, project-triage, RTP_Constraints_Course, SoftwareTech_Review, Tech_Inventory_Analysis, claude-global-memory), one was pushed (graphify-out), and there were no conflicts. Config, skills and memory repos synced, with 7 new memory commits, 10 mods loaded, and 14 projects paired in the memory mirror. The run produced three lessons about how repos come into existence and how the sync can stall.

## Key Points

- **A GitHub repo with no local folder may come from a cloud session.** Of 14 such repos, 12 were archived, one was already local under another name (`AppliedPerformance-Site` as `Website`), and `football-cmj-monitoring` was a new cloud-session `new-project` scaffold. Its `CLAUDE.md` set the folder; it was cloned to `~/DEV/Football/football-cmj-monitoring` and added to `FOOTBALL.md`.
- **Disk-wide searches under `~/DEV` hang.** `find` and loops walk into `_DRIVE`, the Drive symlink, and block on the mount. To find a repo, ask GitHub or use the known repo list.
- **A `*.from-windows` or `*.from-mac` file blocks the project board** until it is moved away, even after its content is merged.
- **Some folders are deliberately not repos.** `SpecialRequests/TOS_ES` holds Athletic Medicine data and stays local. graphify-out is committed after a size check.
- **`where-was-i.py` listed 12 open decisions in 4 repos,** among them whether to rewrite DataBase_GPS_Reporting history to remove `API_Token_FB.txt`.

## Details

Cloud desks add a new way for repos to appear: created on GitHub with no machine involved. The sync's missing-folder list used to mean "archived or renamed." It now also means "new from the cloud," and the scaffold's own `CLAUDE.md` is the cheapest guide to where it belongs. The router file has to be updated at clone time, or the repo is invisible to later sessions.

The `_DRIVE` hang is the same stuck-mount problem that hung `landed.py` and `where-was-i.py --decisions` in closeouts. A symlink into a FUSE mount turns any recursive walk of `~/DEV` into a Drive read. The safe pattern is to query an index (GitHub, the repo list) rather than the filesystem. Leftover conflict files are a different kind of block: the board's loader refuses to start while they are present, so merging the content is not enough; the file has to be moved. PP_Recruiting was picked as the newest project: 024 is a 13-question decisions sheet on the staff Position Grids, 023 is the reviewed grids copy, and next steps are building 025 from the Yes rows and getting Mauro to test 021 in Windows Excel.

# Stuck Google Drive FUSE Mount: Backup Offline Errors and Hanging Readers

On 2026-10-15 and 2026-10-16 the Mac's daily backup failed with `backup-target-offline:GoogleDrive/_MACHINE`. The local Google Drive mount, a FUSE file layer that shows Drive as a folder, was stuck and did not show `_MACHINE/Backups`. While stuck, any script reading Drive hung: `landed.py scan` and `where-was-i.py --decisions` both had to be stopped and skipped at closeout. This confirms the existing Tier A note `drive-fuse-read-hang`. The same day a storage rulebook, `~/.claude/STORAGE.md`, was written to tell agents where each kind of file belongs. By 2026-10-19 the mount still froze on big-file reads, and reading through the Drive API became the recorded default.

## Key Points

- **A stuck mount hangs readers; it does not make them fail.** Scripts that list or read Drive block with no error. Without a timeout, a closeout step simply never returns.
- **The backup error points at the mount, not the backup.** `backup-target-offline` here means the local Drive view is stale. The files were reachable through the API, which was used to upload 5 backup files to `_MACHINE/Backups/gws-upload-2026-10-16/`. The 2026-10-19 closeout confirmed the 10/15 and 10/16 backup failures were this "Google Drive target offline" cause.
- **The Drive API is now the default read path.** On 2026-10-19 a memory note was committed in `~/.claude` making the API the default way to read Drive, and `project_drive-fuse-read-hang.md` was updated, because the Mac folder still freezes on big files. The freeze itself is not fixed.
- **The `.errors.log` entries were kept until the cause was understood,** to be cleared only after a backup succeeds. The 10-19 closeout set the check: after the 9 PM backup, `launchctl list | grep dailybackup` should show 0.
- **Suggested hardening:** a timeout or Drive-offline guard in `landed.py` and `where-was-i.py`.

## Details

Two access paths to the same Drive behaved differently. The API worked: the README fix, closing the Gemini plan and the backup upload all went through it. The FUSE mount did not. Backups and closeout scripts that depend on the mount inherit its health without any sign of it in their own errors, so a backup that looks like it lost its destination is really a local view that stopped updating. The 10-16 decision was to wait for a mount refresh or change the backup to write straight to Google's server (option 2). Three days later the mount had not recovered for large reads, and the response was to change the default for reads rather than keep waiting. This is a policy change, not a fix: tools that walk the mount, such as recursive `find` under `~/DEV` through the `_DRIVE` symlink, still hang.

`STORAGE.md` is the rule side of the same work. It is pointed to from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and allowed through the dotclaude `.gitignore` (commit `93c2d8b`), and a safety check was added to `daily-backup.ps1` (`e3f74fa`). The 10-16 closeout recorded more maintenance debt: four registry drift items, `Cloudroom_Learning` missing from the backup manifest, 1.9 GB of temporary backup files in the session scratchpad, and the startup sync skill committing session history into the dotclaude repo. The PP_Recruiting work on 10-19 showed the practical cost of the freeze: large workbooks had to be read and checked through the API, with uploads verified by matching size.

# Permission Layer Blocking Athlete-Data Verification

On 2026-09-24, a direct check of the S2 data folder on Google Drive was refused by Claude Code's permission layer because the directory listing itself included an athlete-named file. No workaround was attempted; the session reported the block, told the user that a permission rule would be needed to allow such confirmations in future, and recorded the migration's landing state as unconfirmed. The episode is a clean example of an athlete-data guardrail working as designed while imposing a real verification cost.

## Key Points

- **A filename can be the protected content.** The block was triggered not by reading a file's contents but by *listing* a directory, because athlete names appear in the file names — so directory metadata is itself identifiable data under the policy.
- **No circumvention was attempted.** Rather than rerouting through a different tool, a shell glob, or a partial listing, the refusal was accepted and surfaced. Guardrails around athlete and health data are treated as policy, not as obstacles to engineer around.
- **The remedy is an explicit permission rule, not an ad-hoc override.** The user was told that allowing future confirmations requires adding a rule — a deliberate, reviewable configuration change rather than a one-off bypass.
- **The cost is a verification gap, and the gap must be named.** Combined with the same session's reaped background watch, the block left no path to confirm the S2 data had landed on Drive; the outcome was carried into the handoff as unconfirmed rather than assumed.
- **This is the enforcement surface of an existing policy.** The destination-split rule already routes athlete-identifiable data to Drive only and never to GitHub; the permission layer is where that intent becomes mechanical.

## Details

The interesting property of this block is where the sensitivity lives. Most data-governance rules assume the payload is the risk and the path is neutral, which is why gitignoring a `data/` directory is usually sufficient — the files stay out of the remote, and naming them is harmless. Here the inverse held: the request was a listing, the payload was never read, and the identifiable information was carried entirely in the file names. Any tool that enumerates a directory therefore handles athlete-identifiable data, which means the guardrail has to sit at the enumeration boundary rather than only at the read boundary. That is broader than it first appears and explains why an apparently innocuous `ls`-equivalent triggered a refusal.

The response pattern is the transferable part. A blocked operation creates pressure to find an equivalent path — a different tool, a narrower glob, a count instead of a listing — and each of those would technically satisfy the request while defeating the rule's purpose. Declining to look for one, and instead escalating to "a permission rule would be needed," keeps the decision with the person who owns the policy and leaves an auditable record of what was and was not verified. The cost is accepted honestly: the S2 Drive confirmation simply did not happen, and because the background watch that would otherwise have reported the arrival was reaped for memory pressure in the same session, the item left the day as an explicit unknown. An unconfirmed item in a handoff is a better artifact than a confident claim produced by working around a guardrail.

# Connection: Failures That Arrive Together Usually Share One Host Event

## The Connection

On 2026-10-20, two unrelated-looking subsystems failed within minutes: `session-autopush` died with "git-remote-https died of signal 9," and three memory flushes stopped. Earlier closeouts that week saw `daily-backup` fail push and snapshot legs with "Could not resolve host," and Drive-reading checks (`where-was-i.py --decisions`, disk walks into `_DRIVE`) hang at 0% CPU. In every case the subsystem that reported the error was healthy. The host had lost a shared resource: the network, or a responsive Drive mount.

## Key Insight

Earlier articles established that an error names the layer that stopped, and that shutdown or sleep is a cause in its own right. This log adds a diagnostic shortcut: the timing of failures across subsystems is evidence. Two components with no code in common failing in the same window are much more likely to share a dependency than to have two new bugs. Checking the shared dependency first (network, mount, memory, restart time) is cheaper and is usually right. The repair then follows the same pattern each time: confirm the resource is back, re-run the work that left artifacts on disk, and only then clear the logs.

The opposite also holds. A single isolated failure that does not repeat, like the one 10-18 "Control request timeout" flush-error, has no correlated partner and no ongoing cause, so it was left alone rather than investigated.

## Evidence

- Autopush signal-9 failures and three dead flushes both traced to a network drop at about 00:06 local time; one fix (network back, re-run) cleared both.
- `daily-backup` failures on 10-15 to 10-19 logged "Could not resolve host," showing the Mac was offline rather than the backup broken.
- `where-was-i.py --decisions` and recursive `find` under `~/DEV` both hung for the same reason: the stuck Drive FUSE mount behind `_DRIVE`.

# Automated Layout QA Gate for Generated Decks

The layout QA gate is an automated pre-review check in the `Education_Content_Agent` deck pipeline that inspects generated slides for layout defects before a human looks at them. On the 2026-08-19 deck rebuild it caught 8 layout bugs across three direction variants and reported 491 passing checks on the final five-deck build. The session also established the gate's two documented blind spots: it detects box-versus-box collisions but cannot detect text overflowing its own box, and it misread split-layout slides until taught about them.

## Key Points

- **What it catches:** box-versus-box collisions between slide elements. This is a geometric check on element bounding boxes and is reliable within that scope.
- **What it cannot catch:** text overflowing *its own* box. The container's geometry is unchanged when its text spills, so a collision check sees nothing wrong — exactly the defect class that produced the narrow-column heading-into-body-text bug in the Post-Practice deck.
- **False positives from unmodeled layouts:** the gate misread split-layout slides because it could not tell which side of the divide text sat on, generating false positives until it was taught about split layouts. A checker that does not model a layout type will report confidently and wrongly about it.
- **Scale of value:** 8 layout bugs caught pre-review across three variants; 491 checks passed on the final build. The gate's worth is in the volume of mechanical verification it removes from human review, not in completeness.
- **Supporting render path:** `cairosvg` fails on this machine (missing native library), so the working substitute was an HTML contact sheet viewed in Chrome. A PowerPoint-free renderer reading `.pptx` directly was built after PowerPoint automation broke; its preview text spacing is approximate while the `.pptx` files remain exact.

## Details

The gate's blind spots are more instructive than its coverage, because both are failures of *scope* rather than of implementation. Box-versus-box collision detection answers a narrower question than "is this slide laid out correctly": it asks whether two elements overlap, and text spilling past its own container's bounds does not change that container's geometry at all. So the single most common generated-deck defect — content too long for the space allotted — sits precisely in the gate's gap. This is the same shape as a status field that reports accurately on a narrower predicate than the operational question, catalogued in [[connections/status-field-scope-narrower-than-the-question]]: the check is not lying, it is answering a different question than the one being asked of it.

The split-layout false positives are the complementary failure. Because the gate had no model of a hard vertical divide, it could not determine which side of the divide a text element belonged to, and so reported collisions that were not real. An automated checker applied to a layout family it does not model does not fail silently or abstain — it emits confident wrong answers, which is worse than no check, because false positives train the reader to discount the gate's output. Teaching the gate about split layouts was therefore not a nicety but a precondition for the direction change being verifiable at all.

Several supporting-tooling failures in the same session reinforce that the verification path itself must be watched. `cairosvg` could not run for lack of a native library, and the substitute was an HTML contact sheet rendered in Chrome — a lower-tech but working viewport. Silenced or backgrounded regeneration steps hid a failure and served stale SVGs, so regeneration was moved back to running visibly; an edit that stopped `deck_preview` from writing individual SVGs caused the comparison page to read first-run files until it was restored; and `build-all.js` was globbing and executing `build-variants.js` until the glob filter was fixed. Each of these produced output that looked plausible while being stale or wrong, which is the reason the visible-regeneration rule was adopted. Together with the approximate text spacing in the PowerPoint-free preview — accurate enough to judge layout, not accurate enough to judge exact spacing — the session's practical rule is that the gate is a filter that removes mechanical defects before human review, not a substitute for looking at the rendered artifact.

# Auto-Mode Classifier Block: Commit Locally, Do Not Push, Then Ask

On 2026-10-22 at 23:02, a coordinator session on the Mac scaffolded a new repo, `~/DEV/Football/PFF_Position_Reports`. Auto mode's safety classifier blocked two steps: `gh repo create` and the write of `README.md`. The agent did not look for another way to do either step. It finished the local work that was allowed, made a local commit, did not push, and asked Eric. After Eric said "yes", the private GitHub repo was created and the tree ended clean on `main`.

## Key Points

- **Do the local work, commit, stop before the remote step.** The first commit `ae6170b` ("Initial scaffold: AGENTS.md, session routine, gitignore") added `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.gitignore` and `docs/STATUS.md`. Nothing was pushed until Eric approved.
- **Do not route around the block.** Repo creation could have been tried through the GitHub API or a different CLI call, and the README through a shell heredoc. None of these was attempted. A blocked action gets escalated to the user.
- **Approval converts the block into a single action.** Eric's "yes" covered creating the private repo `erash11/PFF_Position_Reports`. The final state was `3d21f30` on `main` with a clean tree.
- **Project instructions override default attribution.** The commits carry no `Co-Authored-By` line, because the project's instructions said not to add one. The project rule took precedence over the harness default.
- **An approval with nothing pending must be clarified.** A later "appoved" message arrived when no step was waiting. The agent asked what it covered instead of applying it to something.

## Details

The pattern splits a task at the point where its effects stop being reversible and local. Scaffolding files and making a local commit can all be undone, and none of it reaches anyone else. Creating a GitHub repo and pushing do reach other people and other machines. Committing locally first has two benefits. The finished work is saved in durable form, so a session that ends while waiting for approval loses nothing. And the request to the user is small and specific: one remote action on work that already exists, not "may I do the whole task."

This matches earlier blocked-action precedents. Auto mode blocked `.claude/` edits during the 2026-06-25 health check, and the classifier blocked `MISSION.md` edits twice on 2026-10-14. In both cases the right response was escalation, not a different tool reaching the same effect. Getting around a classifier with an equivalent command gets the result while defeating the check, which is the same reasoning that kept the athlete-data permission block in place. The narrowest-escalation principle also applies here: what was needed was a single explicit approval for one action, not a wider permission mode.

# Relayed Instructions and Blanket Grants Are Not User Consent

During the 2026-10-21 KeystoneOS repair session the agent applied a consent rule: a note relayed from a coordinator session does not count as approval for a specific consequential action, and neither does a broad grant like "you have full system access." Restoring a launchd plist Eric had deleted and writing to Google Drive both waited until Eric himself gave an unambiguous "yes." Permission changes such as Full Disk Access were left to Eric to make by hand. The next day the rule held in four more sessions. In one, the relay explicitly said "Eric approved these steps." In another, Eric's own message was ambiguous. In a third, an approval arrived when nothing was waiting on it.

## Key Points

- **A relay note reports intent, so it is not consent.** On 2026-10-22 a relay saying "Eric approved these steps" was not acted on. The agent posted a question to the project thread, and the work went ahead only after Eric replied there himself at 14:26Z: "Yes, restore the login, catch up, and run one cloud push."
- **A blanket grant answers whether the agent can act. It does not answer whether it should.** "Full system access" does not name an action, so the agent asks which action the user means.
- **An ambiguous approval from the user still needs clarifying.** Eric's "your preapproved." during the PFF session could have covered a Drive copy or a QB report run. The agent asked "A or B?" and did not pick one.
- **An approval with nothing pending gets a question, not an assignment.** In the 23:02 `PFF_Position_Reports` session, Eric sent "appoved" after the only blocked step had already been approved and done. The agent asked what it was for and did not attach it to some next action.
- **Undoing something the user deliberately did needs fresh approval, and privacy-permission changes stay manual.** The deleted `dailybackup-login.plist` was restored only after Eric's explicit yes. For TCC grants the agent gives the exact binary path and the verification commands, and the human makes the grant.

## Details

The rule matters more as work is split across coordinator and worker sessions. A relayed message loses who said it and exactly what they agreed to. "Eric approved these steps" could be a paraphrase, an inference, or a stale approval that came before a later decision. The 2026-10-22 morning session showed the standard working as intended: the agent did not re-run the cloud push off the automated relay, and waited for Eric's own "go." The 10:38 session took it one step further and sent the confirmation request to a channel Eric reads, so his answer is on record next to the work it authorized.

The PFF sessions showed two more failure modes. In the first, the words came from the user but did not say which action they covered. "your preapproved." could have authorized either of two different actions, and treating it as approval for the riskier reading would be the same mistake as trusting a relay. In the second, "appoved" came in with no step waiting at all. A message like that is the easiest to misuse, because the agent would have to invent the action it authorizes. The usual cause is mundane: a message typed in the wrong thread, or one that arrived after the matter was settled. Asking costs one turn. In practice, consent has to come from the user, name the action it covers, and match an action that is actually pending. When any of those is missing, the agent asks and the action waits. This builds on existing practice: pushes are scoped per repo, destructive git operations need authorization, and authorization is requested again when the diagnosis changes. The new part is a list of inputs that look like approval but are not: relay notes, capability statements, approvals that do not say what they cover, and approvals with nothing to apply to.

- [[concepts/closeout-scope-discipline-other-sessions-work]] - Push authorization scoped per repo.
- [[connections/narrowest-sufficient-escalation-over-blanket-bypass]] - Resolving a blocked action at the narrowest rung.
- [[connections/numbered-approvals-without-their-referents]] - Approvals that become unauditable once their proposal is lost.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms
